name: Meclizine as growth-plate modulator

card.summary: Meclizine is an over-the-counter antihistamine that forum users discuss as a way to loosen a brake on growth-plate cartilage, with the hope of added height while growth plates remain open.
card.aka: Meclizine, meclozine, Bonine, Antivert, Dramamine II
card.note: Studies are in achondroplasia mouse models; no trial has tested it for height in people with typical growth. Drowsiness is common.

quick.overview:
Meclizine is a long-established antihistamine used for motion sickness and vertigo. Height-focused forum members take interest in it because laboratory work reported that it reduces signaling by FGFR3, a receptor that acts as a brake on growth-plate bone lengthening.

The appearance payoff people hope for is extra height. The research behind the idea comes from transgenic mice with achondroplasia and from a small pediatric study in children with that condition; discussion on forums is split between enthusiasts, users trying it as a low-cost experiment, and critics who say the mechanism does not carry over.
quick.how: Forum users describe it as a cheap over-the-counter product tried by people whose growth plates they believe are still open, sometimes alongside other height-related interests. Results are reported only as personal updates; no measured outcomes are available.
quick.risks: Meclizine commonly causes drowsiness, dry mouth and tiredness, and it has anticholinergic effects. It is sold over the counter in the US and Canada and by prescription in Australia [1]. No trial has shown height gain in people with typical growth, and users in the threads themselves call it a long shot.

lead: Meclizine is a first-generation piperazine antihistamine, patented in 1951 and in medical use since 1953, used mainly for motion sickness and vertigo [1]. Among height-focused users it is discussed as a possible growth-plate modulator: the proposed route is lower FGFR3 activity in chondrocytes, which could ease restriction of longitudinal bone growth while growth plates are open [2].

The idea traces to laboratory work by a Japanese research group (Matsushita and colleagues) using mice carrying an achondroplasia mutation, which reported that clinical-range doses of meclozine, the spelling those papers use, promoted longitudinal bone growth. A phase Ia study in children with achondroplasia reported that it was well tolerated. These studies concern a condition with overactive FGFR3, not typical growth.
On looksmax.org, threads range from detailed mechanism posts to a thread titled as a warning that it will not add height, and a user who started taking it and said they would report back [2][3][4].

chain: Meclizine dampens FGFR3 signaling in growth-plate cells (lab studies)
Possible faster bone lengthening while plates are open
angle.text: Users who believe their growth plates are open try it hoping for extra longitudinal growth. The pathway is drawn from mouse and achondroplasia research and has not been demonstrated for typical height.

infobox: Bonine, Antivert, Dramamine II, Sea Legs [1]
OTC in US and Canada; Rx in Australia [1]

paras: Meclizine treats nausea, vomiting and dizziness from motion sickness and may be used for vertigo, including that of Meniere's disease; it is also considered a first-line option for nausea in pregnancy [1].

Forum posters describe FGFR3 as the main negative regulator of growth-plate bone lengthening and say reducing its activity widens the proliferative zone and increases growth velocity while plates remain open, without affecting plate closure [3]. Others dispute the mechanism, arguing that bone growth is governed mainly by the CNP-NPR-B-cGMP pathway and that nothing shows meclizine acts there [2]. One user describes starting it while expecting that benefit is unlikely, citing mouse studies [4].

Meclizine blocks H1 histamine receptors and has anticholinergic, sedating and local anesthetic effects; oral bioavailability is roughly 22-32%, peak levels come in about 1.5 hours and it is processed in the liver by CYP2D6 [1].
Common effects are drowsiness, dry mouth and tiredness; serious allergic reactions are unlikely [1].

Research on meclozine and growth comes from transgenic achondroplasia mice, where a Japanese group reported FGFR3 suppression in chondrocytes and improved long-bone growth, and from a phase Ia pharmacokinetic and safety study in children with achondroplasia that reported good tolerability [1]. No trials in people with typical growth have measured height.

lore.intro: The topic appears in height threads on looksmax.org as both a hopeful mechanism and a contested claim [2][3][4].

claims.claim: Meclizine suppresses FGFR3 and so removes a brake on growth plates
claims.believers: Proponents cite mouse studies showing FGFR3 downregulation in growth-plate chondrocytes and say this lets bones lengthen while plates are open [3].
claims.experts: The mouse work used achondroplasia models with overactive FGFR3; a pediatric study in achondroplasia reported tolerability. No trial in typical growth has measured height.

claims.claim: Meclizine cannot add height because growth is controlled by CNP signaling
claims.believers: Critics argue that CNP, NPR-B and cGMP drive plate growth and that FGFR3 inhibition would not change normal height [2].
claims.experts: No published study has tested meclizine's effect on height in people without achondroplasia.
